title: Under the blanket
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative, not targets; your unit’s protocol and the physician’s orders come first.
intro: Mr. Ernesto Villar, 74, dialyzes through a left forearm fistula. He is hard of hearing and dozes during treatment. The unit is cold today. On your rounds at 1 hour 10 minutes you find him asleep, with a thick blanket pulled up to his chin and over his access arm. His fluid goal is 2.8 liters over 4 hours.

n1.prompt: What do you do about the blanket?

choices.text: Fold the blanket back so the access arm, needles, and line connections are in view, tape and check them, and tuck the blanket over the rest of his body.
choices.feedback: The access and every connection should stay visible for the whole session. A blanket hides the one cause of sudden blood loss you can see directly. He can stay warm with his arm in view.
choices.then: The needles are taped and secure. You tell him, loudly and kindly, why his arm must stay uncovered. He nods and falls asleep again.

choices.text: Leave it. He is cold and comfortable, and the machine will alarm if anything happens.
choices.feedback: A venous needle can come out without a pressure alarm. The venous pressure may fall only a little, inside the alarm limits. The machine is not a substitute for seeing the access.
choices.then: You move on to the next station.

choices.text: Lift the edge, glance at the needles, and put the blanket back over the arm.
choices.feedback: Checking is right, but a covered arm stays hidden between checks. The safer habit is to keep the access in view all the time.
choices.then: The needles look secure. The blanket goes back over his arm.

n2.scene: Later in the shift, your colleague Ms. Grace Manalo calls out. Mr. Villar is pale and hard to rouse. There is a dark, spreading wet patch on the bedding by his access arm. The venous needle is lying outside the skin. The machine has not alarmed.

choices.text: Stop the blood pump, clamp the lines, press firmly on the site with gloved hand and gauze, and call for help.
choices.feedback: Stop the loss first. While the pump runs, blood keeps leaving through the open circuit. Firm direct pressure controls the needle site.

choices.text: Look at the machine to find out why it did not alarm, then stop it.
choices.feedback: The machine can be investigated later. Every second it runs, it pumps blood out of a disconnected line.
choices.then: Ms. Manalo stops the pump and clamps the lines while you press on the site.

choices.text: Push the venous needle back into the fistula to restore the circuit.
choices.feedback: A needle that has been out of the skin is contaminated and may be in the wrong place. Reinserting it risks infection and infiltration, and it delays stopping the loss.
choices.then: Ms. Manalo stops the pump and clamps the lines. You discard the needle and press on the site.

n3.scene: The bleeding is controlled under pressure. Help has arrived.

choices.text: Lay him flat, check consciousness, breathing, pulse, and blood pressure, and estimate the blood loss from the bedding and floor.
choices.feedback: His low pressure and fast pulse point to blood loss. Lying flat returns blood to the heart. The estimate of blood loss is what the physician needs to decide on fluid and further care.
choices.then: He opens his eyes to his name. His pressure is 92/54 lying flat. The soaked bedding and pads suggest about 400 mL.

choices.text: Sit him upright so he can talk to you more easily.
choices.feedback: Talking to him checks his responsiveness, but sitting up drops his pressure further after blood loss. Lay him flat first.
choices.then: He becomes gray when sat up. You lay him flat. His pressure is 92/54 lying down. The bedding suggests about 400 mL lost.

choices.text: Change the soaked bedding first so you can see the arm properly.
choices.feedback: The soaked bedding is your best estimate of how much blood he lost. Assess the patient first, estimate from the bedding, then change it.
choices.then: You stop and assess him. Lying flat, his pressure is 92/54. The bedding you nearly discarded suggests about 400 mL.

n4.prompt: A colleague asks whether to return the blood in the circuit through the venous line. What do you say?

choices.text: Not through a line end that has been open. Whether any blood is returned, and how, follows the unit’s protocol and the physician’s direction.
choices.feedback: The venous line lay open on the bedding, so it may be contaminated. Blood is not returned through a line end that has been open. The physician decides on fluid and any return by another route.

choices.text: Yes, reconnect the venous line to the needle and return it. He needs the volume.
choices.feedback: He does need volume, but not through a contaminated open line. That risks a bloodstream infection in a patient who is already unstable. The physician directs fluid replacement.

choices.text: Leave the circuit clamped and ask the physician.
choices.feedback: Asking the physician is right. Know the reason too: blood is not returned through a line end that has been open.

n5.prompt: What do you tell the nephrologist?

choices.text: Venous needle dislodgement found at 2 h 35 min, about 400 mL estimated loss, treatment stopped with 1.7 of 2.8 L removed, current vital signs and responsiveness, what was done, and the plan for disposition.
choices.feedback: The handoff states what was delivered and how he is, not only that an event happened. The nephrologist needs the delivered time and volume to decide whether he needs another session, and the blood loss to decide on fluid and tests.

choices.text: That his needle came out and he bled, and that he is now stable.
choices.feedback: True, but too little to act on. Give the estimated blood loss, the time delivered against the time prescribed, the fluid removed against the goal, and his current vital signs.

choices.text: Nothing yet; write the incident report first, then call.
choices.feedback: The call comes first. The patient may need fluid, tests, or transfer now. The report is written once he is safe.

end.title: After the event
end.text: The nephrologist orders fluid under protocol and a hemoglobin check, and arranges his next session. When he is settled, you explain again why his access arm must stay uncovered and ask him to report dizziness or wetness at once. The record states delivered time, fluid removed, estimated blood loss, his status, and who was informed. The incident report gives the facts and times without blame, and the team asks why the machine did not alarm.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Keep the access in view. Warm the patient, not the needles. A covered arm hides the one cause of sudden blood loss you can see.
  • Do not trust the alarm. A venous needle can come out without a pressure alarm.
  • Stop the loss first: stop the pump, clamp, press, call for help. Then lay the patient flat and assess.
  • Never return blood through a line end that has been open. Fluid and any return follow protocol and the physician.
  • Report what was delivered: time on treatment against time prescribed, fluid removed against the goal, estimated blood loss, and current status.

See First actions while help is coming.
